lesson.title: Many Ways to Build a Dictionary
lesson.summary: Python offers several ways to construct a dictionary, including curly-brace literals, the dict() constructor, and dictionary comprehensions, and choosing between them is a matter of which is clearest for the data you already have.
lesson.body:
Dictionaries showed the most common way to build a dictionary: writing it directly with curly braces and key: value pairs. That literal syntax is the right choice when you already know the data by hand, but Python provides other ways to build a dictionary that fit better when your data starts out in a different shape.

The dict() constructor can build a dictionary from keyword arguments, dict(x=1, y=2), which is convenient when keys are simple names known ahead of time, or from a list of two-item pairs, dict([("x", 1), ("y", 2)]), which is convenient when the data already exists as pairs, perhaps read from a file or produced by another part of a program. A third option, dict.fromkeys(some_list, default_value), builds a dictionary from a list of keys, assigning the same starting value to every one of them, useful for initializing a tally or a set of flags before filling in real values later.

a = {"x": 1, "y": 2}
b = dict(x=1, y=2)
c = dict([("x", 1), ("y", 2)])
d = dict.fromkeys(["x", "y"], 0)

print(a == b == c)
print(d)

The first print shows True: all three of a, b, and c describe the identical dictionary, {'x': 1, 'y': 2}, just built through different syntax. The second print shows {'x': 0, 'y': 0}, both keys present with the same default value 0 supplied to fromkeys().

A fourth option worth knowing is the dictionary comprehension, which mirrors a list comprehension's compact for-loop syntax but produces key-value pairs instead of single values: {k: k * k for k in range(1, 5)} produces {1: 1, 2: 4, 3: 9, 4: 16}. One detail applies no matter which method you use to build a dictionary: keys must stay unique. If a key is written twice in a literal, {"x": 1, "x": 2}, Python keeps only the last value assigned to it, silently discarding the earlier one, so the result is simply {'x': 2}, not an error and not both values somehow combined.
